rows.evidence: Q1: Methods section (Remote Sensing Monitoring; Environmental and Social Data Collection; Field Survey) - authors classify Landsat TM/ETM+ images for 1995-2010, validate with field surveys (overall accuracy 95.1%, Kappa 0.898), and analyse runoff, groundwater table data from 59 wells (1998-2011), and biyearly field surveys 2005-2013.
rows.notes: The study uses remote sensing only as the researchers' own monitoring tool to map land use change (Tables 1-4, Figs 2-3). It does not report that RS data were used by policy makers to set water quotas or reduce irrigated area, and it does not test RS as a technology producing groundwater recovery. The groundwater table rise of 45 cm (2005-2011, northern oasis) and the increase in inflow (Fig. 4; Discussion, 'Impacts of Policies') are attributed to the Ecological Construction policy measures (closing 3,161 wells, water allocation plan requiring 22% of mountain runoff to reach Minqin, drip/tube irrigation, reduced irrigated area), measured from well and gauge records, not from RS. RS here is upstream (monitoring/mapping) of the claimed effect; no causal link from RS to groundwater recharge is established.

rows.evidence: Q1: Methods section - own Landsat image classification for 1995, 2000, 2005, 2010 validated by field survey and confusion matrix; own field surveys 2005-2013 in 125 villages.
rows.notes: The study's own RS result on vegetation is an area change of land-cover classes (Table 1: shrub land 116.71 km2 in 2005 to 160.10 km2 in 2010; tree land declining), which the authors attribute to afforestation campaigns under the EC policy, not to any use of remote sensing. Statements on vegetation types falling from 19 to 9 varieties and on community composition shifts are cited from other work (Wang et al. 2002; Peng et al. 2004; Li et al. 2011) and do not count. No result links RS as a technology to biodiversity or vegetation recovery; RS is only the mapping method (upstream of the claimed effect). Note also that vegetation cover change is not biodiversity.

rows.evidence: Q1: Methods section - own remote sensing classification, hydrological and groundwater records (Shiyang River Basin Management Bureau, Water Resource Bureau of Minqin County), and field surveys 2005-2013.
rows.notes: Water-saving outcomes reported in the Discussion ('Impacts of Policies') - irrigation water efficiency rising from 0.56 (2006) to 0.61 (2010), water consumption reduced by 1500 m3/ha for grain and 1800 m3/ha for cash crops, groundwater extraction down 2.4x10^8 m3 - are attributed to the EC policy package (drip and tube irrigation on half the irrigated area, closing wells, crop restructuring, watershed water allocation) and come from county bureau statistics, not from RS. The study never reports that RS data were used to set water quotas or that RS produced water conservation; its RS component only maps land-use change. The claim's technology-effect link is not tested; RS is upstream (monitoring).

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is a primary land-use/policy case study of Minqin Oasis using Landsat classification plus hydrological, groundwater, climate and socio-economic records and field surveys. Remote sensing is the authors' analytical tool for mapping land-use change; the review's framing that conservation policies 'used RS data to set water quotas' is not supported by anything the study reports. The positive outcomes (groundwater rise, inflow increase, water-use efficiency, shrub land increase) are attributed to policy measures (well closures, water allocation, drip/tube irrigation, afforestation), so all three rows fail Q2 with upstream=true.
